q.intro.text: A patio is a twelve foot by eight foot rectangle, with a half circle on one eight foot end. Flexible edging will go all the way around its edge.

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one: the picture moves first, then the notation.

e.s1.text: Split it: a twelve by eight rectangle and a half circle. They meet along the dashed seam, so the half circle's diameter is the eight foot side, and its radius is four feet.

e.s2.text: Area: add the parts. The rectangle is twelve times eight. The half circle is half of pi times four squared. Together, ninety-six plus eight pi square feet: the stones for the patio.

e.s3.text: Perimeter: walk around the edge once. Twelve, the curved edge, twelve, eight. The curve is half of a circle with diameter eight: half of eight pi, which is four pi. The seam is inside the patio, so the edging never touches it.

e.s4.text: Combine like terms: thirty-two plus four pi feet, exactly. Round only at the end: with pi about three point one four, that is about forty-four point six feet of edging.

e.why.text: Quick check. Why is the eight foot seam not part of the edging?

e.w-ok.text: Yes. The seam is where the two parts meet, inside the patio. Walking around the edge, you never step on it.

e.w-seam.text: Not every line in a drawing is an edge. The seam only shows where the parts meet. The edging runs along the outside.

e.w-across.text: The curve bends out, so it is longer than the straight eight feet: half of eight pi, about twelve point six feet. And the seam still is not on the edge.

t.intro.text: A flower bed is shaped like a running track: a fourteen foot by eight foot rectangle, with a half circle on each eight foot end. Edging goes around it.

t.s1.text: Split it: a rectangle and two half circles, each with diameter eight, so radius four feet.

t.s2.text: Area: fourteen times eight, plus two half circles, which make one whole circle: pi times four squared. That is one hundred twelve plus sixteen pi square feet of soil.

t.walk.text: Your step. Which pieces does the edging run along?

t.w-ok.text: Yes. Two straight sides and two curves. The two eight foot seams are inside the bed.

t.w-seam.text: The two eight foot lines are seams, inside the bed where the parts meet. The edging never runs there.

t.w-curve.text: The curved ends are edges too. The edging bends around them.

t.exact.text: Now write the perimeter exactly: a number part, plus a pi part.

t.e-ok.text: Yes. Fourteen plus fourteen is twenty-eight, and each curve is half of eight pi, so the two make eight pi: twenty-eight plus eight pi feet.

t.e-half.text: That is one curve. There are two, and together they make a whole circle's circumference.

t.e-area.text: Pi times four squared is the circle's area. The edge is the circumference: pi times eight.

t.e-unlike.text: Twenty-eight is not a pi term, so it cannot join eight pi. Keep them apart.

t.e-seam.text: That has the two eight foot seams in it. They are inside the bed. Leave them out.

t.e-no.text: Add the straight sides. Then the two curves, each half of pi times eight.

t.round.text: About how many feet is that? Round to the nearest tenth, at the end.

t.r-ok.text: Yes. Twenty-eight plus eight pi is about fifty-three point one feet of edging.

t.r-unlike.text: That is thirty-six pi. Only the eight is multiplied by pi. Work out eight pi first, then add twenty-eight.

t.r-early.text: Pi was rounded too early. Keep three point one four, or the pi key, and round only the final answer.

t.r-no.text: Eight pi is about twenty-five point one three. Add twenty-eight, then round to the nearest tenth.

t.cb-right.text: At the start you picked thirty-two plus four pi feet, and you were right. Now you can show why.

t.cb-seam.text: At the start you picked forty plus four pi feet. That walks along the seam. The seam is inside, so the edging is thirty-two plus four pi feet.

t.cb-curve.text: At the start you picked thirty-two feet. That leaves out the curved edge. The edging bends around it too: thirty-two plus four pi feet.

p.intro.text: Riley says: cut a piece out of a shape, and its perimeter always gets smaller. Test it. A ten foot by six foot table top gets a half circle notch, of radius two feet, cut into one long side.

p.test.text: Let's test it. Build the argument, and see where it leads.

p.prove.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.c1.text: The notch takes away four feet of straight edge,

p.c2.text: but it adds a curved edge of two pi feet, about six point three feet,

p.c3.text: so the perimeter goes up, from thirty-two to twenty-eight plus two pi, about thirty-four point three feet, while the area goes down. Riley is wrong.

p.x-shrink.text: The cut also makes a new edge, all along the curve. That edge counts.

p.x-together.text: That is Riley's idea, the one being tested. A rule that says always needs to hold for every shape.

p.x-across.text: The curve bends, so it is longer than the straight gap: half of four pi, about six point three feet.

p.x-other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line.

p.done.text: That's a proof by counterexample. One cut that makes the perimeter longer is enough to break always.
